text: A Virtual Machine Scale Set deploys and manages a group of identical, load-balanced VM instances as a single resource, instead of you creating and tracking each VM one at a time by hand. Every instance in the set shares the same image and size, with a load balancer or application gateway in front spreading incoming traffic across whichever instances happen to be running at that moment.

az vmss create sets up the whole group at once: an image, a VM size, a starting instance count, and the load balancer it sits behind. From there, the instance count can be changed manually by an administrator, but the real value comes from autoscale, which changes it automatically based on actual measured demand instead of a guess made in advance of traffic ever arriving.

Autoscale watches a metric, most commonly CPU percentage though memory and custom metrics work too, and compares it against thresholds you define. A typical rule scales out by one instance when average CPU stays above 70% for 10 minutes, and scales back in once it drops below 30%. A minimum and maximum instance count keep the set from shrinking below what availability requires or growing past a cost ceiling you've set.

Real traffic to most applications spikes during busy periods, like business hours or a marketing push, and falls off overnight. Sizing fixed, always-on capacity for that peak wastes money every single quiet hour; sizing for the average instead means the application falls over the moment a spike hits. A scale set with autoscale solves both problems at once — it runs the minimum during quiet periods and adds instances automatically, usually within minutes, when load actually increases, then removes them again once load drops.

Scale sets can also be spread across the Availability Zones from earlier in this chapter, combining automatic scaling with datacenter-level resilience in one deployment. That closes out VM compute for this chapter — sizing, resilience with sets and zones, disk tiers, and now automatic scaling.
